moduleMetadata.title: Email & Business Communication Security
moduleMetadata.description: Identify and prevent sophisticated email-based threats like Business Email Compromise (BEC) and executive impersonation.
moduleMetadata.whyThisMatters: Email is one of the most important communication tools used by organizations. Because email is so widely used, attackers often target it. A malicious email may attempt to steal credentials, deliver malware, redirect payments, obtain confidential information, or impersonate an executive.
moduleMetadata.learningOutcome: Users should understand how to communicate securely and identify common email-based business threats.

learningObjectives: Identify Business Email Compromise (BEC) and executive impersonation tactics.
Verify senders and recognize look-alike domains.
Safely handle suspicious attachments and links in a business context.
Recognize fraudulent requests for bank detail or payment modifications.
Apply safe use of CC and BCC fields and manage misaddressed emails.

sections.title: Business Email Compromise (BEC)
sections.content: BEC is a sophisticated scam where an attacker impersonates a business associate or executive to trick employees into transferring funds or revealing sensitive data.

subsections.title: Executive Impersonation
subsections.content: An attacker sends an email appearing to be from the CEO or a Director, often requesting 'urgent' help with a task or a payment.

subsections.title: The Fake Invoice
subsections.content: An attacker impersonates a supplier and sends an invoice with 'updated' bank account details for payment.

sections.title: Advanced Sender Verification
sections.content: Don't trust the 'Display Name'. Always check the actual email address.
bulletPoints: Unusual sender: A request from an external address claiming to be internal.

sections.title: Secure Communication Practices
sections.content: How you manage recipients can prevent data leakage.

subsections.title: CC vs. BCC
subsections.content: Use CC (Carbon Copy) when everyone needs to see who else is on the thread. Use BCC (Blind Carbon Copy) to hide recipient addresses, especially for large external groups.

subsections.title: Misaddressed Emails
subsections.content: Always double-check the 'To' field. Auto-complete can easily insert the wrong person with a similar name.

sections.title: Verifying Unusual Requests
sections.content: If a request involves money, sensitive data, or bypassing procedures, verify it through a secondary channel (e.g., a phone call or a new, separate email to a known address).
sections.rule: Never use the contact details provided in the suspicious email itself.

interactiveExercises.title: Email Verification
interactiveExercises.question: Which of these sender addresses is most likely a look-alike domain for 'security@bank-example.com'?
interactiveExercises.explanation: Replacing a 'l' with a '1' is a common tactic to trick the eye.

interactiveExercises.title: Red Flags Detection
interactiveExercises.question: Identify the red flags in this 'CEO' email: 'I'm in a secret meeting and need you to buy $500 in gift cards for a client. Don't call me, just reply with the codes. Hurry!'

scenarios.title: The Manager's PDF
scenarios.content: You receive an unexpected attachment 'Project_Update.pdf' from your manager's real email address, but the text is very short and generic.
scenarios.action: Call your manager to verify. Their account may have been compromised and is now sending malware to contacts.
scenarios.lesson: Compromised accounts can send malicious mail from 'trusted' addresses.

choices.text: Open the PDF — it came from your manager's real email address
choices.consequence: A compromised mailbox can send from the real address. PDFs and other attachments are a common malware delivery channel, and opening one executes the payload.

choices.text: Reply asking if the attachment is legitimate
choices.consequence: The reply goes to the compromised mailbox. The attacker will say "yes, please open it" and you will trust them because the reply came from the real address.

choices.text: Call your manager on a known number to verify before opening anything
choices.consequence: A two-minute call bypasses the compromised mailbox entirely. If it is legitimate, you open it safely later; if not, you just prevented a malware execution.

choices.text: Forward it to a coworker to check if it is safe
choices.consequence: You just distributed a potentially malicious attachment to another inbox. If either of you opens it, the malware has a new foothold.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Call your manager on a known number to verify before opening anything

scenarios.title: The Supplier Invoice
scenarios.content: A regular supplier emails: 'Our bank is being audited. Please send all future payments to this new account number.'
scenarios.action: Do NOT pay. Call the supplier on their known, official number to verify the change.
scenarios.lesson: Financial detail changes must always be verified out-of-band.

choices.text: Update the supplier's bank details and pay the next invoice to the new account
choices.consequence: Your payment goes to the attacker. Invoice fraud is one of the costliest attacks on businesses — once the wire leaves your bank, recovery is rarely full.

choices.text: Reply to the email asking for confirmation on the new account
choices.consequence: The reply goes back to the compromised mailbox. The attacker will confirm their own account and you will have a false sense of verification.

choices.text: Call the supplier on the phone number you already have on file to verify the change out-of-band
choices.consequence: An out-of-band call to a number you already trust confirms with the real supplier. Never use contact details included in the suspicious request itself.

choices.text: Pay half the invoice to the new account as a test
choices.consequence: You still sent money to the attacker. A "test payment" is still a successful fraud — just a smaller one.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Call the supplier on the phone number you already have on file to verify the change out-of-band

scenarios.title: The CEO Gift Card Request
scenarios.content: The CEO emails you (a junior staff member) directly, asking for an urgent favor while they are 'busy in a meeting'.
scenarios.action: Be highly skeptical. CEOs rarely ask junior staff for urgent financial favors via email.
scenarios.lesson: Attackers target staff who might be intimidated by authority.

choices.text: Buy the gift cards and reply with the codes — the CEO is waiting
choices.consequence: Gift card codes are effectively cash. Once sent, the attacker redeems them within minutes and the money is unrecoverable.

choices.text: Verify the request through a separate channel (call the CEO's assistant, or the CEO directly on a known number)
choices.consequence: Executive-impersonation fraud depends on you not checking. A quick call to a trusted channel is exactly what the attacker is counting on you skipping.

choices.text: Reply to the email asking for more details
choices.consequence: You are still negotiating with the attacker. They will add more urgency and authority to push you to buy the cards before you think it through.

choices.text: Forward the request to a coworker and ask them to handle it
choices.consequence: You pass the trap to someone who may be less skeptical. The attack now has two chances to succeed inside your organization.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Verify the request through a separate channel (call the CEO's assistant, or the CEO directly on a known number)

scenarios.title: CC vs BCC Risk
scenarios.content: You need to send an update to 200 external customers. You put all their addresses in the 'CC' field.
scenarios.impact: Privacy violation. Every customer can now see every other customer's email address.
scenarios.action: Use BCC for large external distributions.
scenarios.lesson: BCC protects the privacy of recipients.

choices.text: Send the email as-is with all addresses in CC
choices.consequence: Every recipient now has the full list of 200 customer email addresses. This is a privacy breach that can trigger regulatory fines (GDPR, local equivalents) and erode customer trust.

choices.text: Move all recipient addresses to BCC before sending
choices.consequence: BCC hides the recipient list from each recipient. The message reaches everyone, and no customer learns who else is on the distribution.

choices.text: Send the email to yourself and forward it to each customer individually
choices.consequence: Tedious and error-prone — and if you later use Reply-All on any thread, you recreate the same privacy breach you were trying to avoid.

choices.text: Post the update on a public webpage and email the link
choices.consequence: Publicly posting customer-directed content may be fine, but it depends on what the update contains. Customer-specific or sensitive information should not be made public.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Move all recipient addresses to BCC before sending

quiz.question: What does BEC stand for?
quiz.explanation: BEC is a type of fraud that targets organizations.

quiz.question: Why do attackers impersonate executives?
options: To use the executive's authority to pressure staff into making mistakes.
To get better at their jobs.
quiz.correctAnswer: To use the executive's authority to pressure staff into making mistakes.
quiz.explanation: People are more likely to bypass procedures if they think the boss is asking.

quiz.question: A 'Look-alike Domain' is:
options: An email domain that looks very similar to a legitimate one (e.g., mircosoft.com).
A domain that has a lot of pictures.
quiz.correctAnswer: An email domain that looks very similar to a legitimate one (e.g., mircosoft.com).
quiz.explanation: These are used to trick users into thinking a message is from a trusted source.

quiz.question: What is the best way to verify a request to change a supplier's bank details?
options: Reply to the email and ask for confirmation.
Call the supplier using a trusted phone number you already have.
Just make the change, it's probably fine.
quiz.correctAnswer: Call the supplier using a trusted phone number you already have.
quiz.explanation: Never use contact information provided within a suspicious request.

quiz.question: When should you use the BCC field?
options: When you want everyone to see who you are emailing.
When you want to hide the list of recipients from each other.
When you are only emailing one person.
When you want to highlight a specific person.
quiz.correctAnswer: When you want to hide the list of recipients from each other.
quiz.explanation: BCC (Blind Carbon Copy) ensures privacy by hiding other recipients' addresses.

quiz.question: Executive impersonation often includes a request for:
quiz.explanation: These are hard-to-trace methods of moving money.

quiz.question: What is 'Misaddressed Email' risk?
options: The email taking too long to arrive.
Accidentally sending sensitive information to the wrong person due to auto-complete or typos.
The email getting lost in spam.
The email having a bad subject line.
quiz.correctAnswer: Accidentally sending sensitive information to the wrong person due to auto-complete or typos.
quiz.explanation: This is a common cause of accidental data breaches.

quiz.question: An email from 'billing@amazon-support.co' (instead of .com) is likely a:
options: Phishing attempt using a look-alike domain.
quiz.correctAnswer: Phishing attempt using a look-alike domain.
quiz.explanation: Slight variations in the top-level domain (.co vs .com) are red flags.

keyTakeaways: Verify the sender's actual email address, not just the name.
Be wary of urgent requests for money or sensitive data.
Verify financial changes through a secondary, trusted channel.
Use BCC for large distributions to protect privacy.
reflectApply: Check your 'Sent' folder. Have you used CC when BCC would have been more private?
If you received a request for a 'secret' wire transfer from your CEO right now, what would you do?
